newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli 1997 budget vulnerable to slowing economy.
newsitem.headline: Israeli 1997 budget vulnerable to slowing economy.

text.p: By backing down on key points in its 1997 budget, Israel's Treasury has cleared the way to win approval of its spending package but it now faces a tougher battle than before to keep the deficit on target, analysts warn.
"The 2.8 percent deficit target will be very difficult to keep," said Adam Reuter of Financial Immunities, a consulting firm.

Although Reuter expressed satisfaction with the cuts and revenue-raising measures approved on Sunday by the parliamentary finance committee, he said the the slowing economy would make it difficult for the government to meet tax revenue targets.
The parliamentary finance committee approved the Arrangements Law, which enacts legislative changes needed to fulfil the budget and contained the Treasury's most controversial proposals.

To win approval, however, the Treasury backed down on its plans to reduce child allowances, impose fees for doctors' visits and raise medicine prices. Instead, it agreed to the committee's demand to raise taxes on cigarettes and petrol and approved a plan not to adjust income tax brackets for inflation. The latter will effectively raise income tax.
The panel did agree to cut government investment subsidies to a ceiling of 24 percent, down from the current 34 percent but less than the 20 percent the Treasury sought.

By agreeing to the changes, analysts said, the Treasury succumbed to budgetary opponents who said the brunt of the cuts and revenue-raising measures fell on lower-income groups. The Arrangements Law and the budget are now both expected to win full parliamentary approval by December 31.

"The fact that those two items (child allowances and physicians' fees) were replaced by higher cigarette and fuel taxes and a freezing of brackets is no big deal," said Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets. "The doctor fees was a tax by any other name."

But Yoram Gabbay, chairman of Peilim fund managers and a former Treasury budget director, warned that the "tax component of the new budget is not small," making the budget vulernable to a slowing economy.

The planned cuts in the defence budget, he added, were not realistic. "With the current political ststus quo, there is a good chance of a heating up with the Syrians or the Palestinians," Gabbay said. That would require stepped-up defence spending.
Out of the seven billion shekel budget package, Finance Minister Dan Meridor claimed to have won spending cuts of five billion shekels.
"That's what Meridor is saying but my gut feeling is that it is less than five billion," said Katz. Gabbay said the cuts would be no more than four billion shekels.

Katz nevertheless remained optimistic. "The important thing for the economy is that what happened in 1996 won't happen in 1997," said Katz, adding that lower inflation than the Treasury foresaw when it did its original budget estimates last June would help reduce spending.

This year the Treasury overestimated tax revenues by some five billion shekels, Katz said, as economic growth fell to an estimated 3.8 percent from 7.1 percent in 1995. That caused the deficit to widen to 3.5-4.0 percent of gross domestic product, versus a planned 2.5 percent.

Analysts are divided about how the budget will influence interest rates. Reuter said the Bank of Israel would cut rates 1.2-1.5 percentage point over the next three months. But Gabbay was less optimistic. "The rate cuts will be lower than expected on the basis of a full budget cut," he said. "Real interest rates will be high all year."
Katz said Bank of Israel Governor Jacob Frenkel was more geared towards hard economic data than fiscal promises.
"I think he's more realistic than in the past," Katz said. "I don't see him doing a drastic lowering of interest rates as he did in 1995 -- certainly not on the basis of a planned budget cut."
